subject: physics

items.q: The specification says that diverse phenomena can be described in terms of a small number of key ideas. Which statement best describes a key idea in physics?
items.correct: A way of thinking that recurs in many topics and describes a wide range of phenomena
items.misconception: An especially large and detailed topic that has to be revised in far more depth
items.why: Students equate importance with the amount of detail they have to learn. A small number of key ideas describe a very wide range of phenomena. Their value lies in how widely they apply, not in how much detail they contain.
items.random_wrong: A rule that applies only inside the topic in which it was first taught

items.q: The key ideas are of universal application and are embedded throughout the subject content. What does this mean for the examinations?
items.correct: They can be assessed in questions on any topic, on all papers
items.misconception: They are examined only in the last question of the final paper
items.why: The key ideas are not set out as a teaching topic with their own content list, so students treat them as preamble. Because they are of universal application, questions on any topic and on any paper can require them.
items.random_wrong: They are examined only in questions set for the higher tier

items.q: Which of the following does the specification list as a key idea in physics?
items.correct: The use of models, such as the particle model of matter
items.misconception: Learning the names of all the required practical activities
items.why: Students equate importance with the amount of detail they have to learn. A small number of key ideas describe a very wide range of phenomena. Their value lies in how widely they apply, not in how much detail they contain.
items.random_wrong: Quoting every calculated answer to three significant figures

items.q: Why is the particle model of matter called a model?
items.correct: Because it is a simplified way to explain and predict
items.misconception: Because it is a physical copy of matter built for classroom use
items.why: In everyday language a model is a scaled-down object, and the first models many students meet in school are physical demonstrations. The particle model of matter and the wave models of light and of sound are ideas, not objects. They earn their place because they explain observations and predict new ones.
items.random_wrong: Because it is an idea that no evidence has yet been found for

items.q: Light and sound are both described using a wave model. Which statement about these two models is correct?
items.correct: Sound is modelled as a longitudinal wave and light as a transverse wave
items.misconception: Sound and light are both modelled as longitudinal waves in a medium
items.why: Diagrams show sound as a wavy oscilloscope trace, which looks transverse even though the oscillation is along the direction of travel. The oscilloscope trace is a graph of pressure against time, not a picture of the wave. In sound the particles oscillate along the direction of energy transfer, so the wave is longitudinal.
items.random_wrong: Sound and light are both modelled as transverse waves on a screen

items.q: A car on a straight road has a constant resultant force acting forwards. Using the idea of cause and effect, what is the effect of that force?
items.correct: The car accelerates for as long as the force acts on it
items.misconception: The car keeps moving at a steady speed while the force acts
items.why: Everyday experience involves friction, so a steady push really does give a steady speed and things really do stop when you stop pushing. In those everyday cases the resultant force is zero, because friction balances the push. A non-zero resultant force is the cause and acceleration is the effect.
items.random_wrong: The car gains mass steadily while the force is applied

items.q: A sample of an unstable isotope emits alpha particles. Applying the idea of cause and effect, what is the cause of this emission?
items.correct: A change inside the nucleus of the atom
items.misconception: A chemical reaction between the outer electrons
items.why: Almost every other change students meet, such as melting, dissolving and burning, is controlled by external conditions, so they transfer that expectation to decay. Radioactive decay is a nuclear process. Heating, cooling or chemically reacting a sample does not change its rate of decay, because the cause lies inside the nucleus.
items.random_wrong: The high temperature of the material around it

items.q: Two magnets repel each other without touching. Which group of effects does physics analyse using the idea of a field?
items.misconception: Gravitational, frictional and elastic contact effects
items.why: Students group all forces together and do not separate contact forces from non-contact forces. Fields are used for the non-contact effects: electrical, magnetic and gravitational. Friction and air resistance act only where surfaces are in contact.
items.random_wrong: Electrical, magnetic and thermal conduction effects

items.q: Which statement correctly applies the key idea that differences are the drivers of change?
items.correct: Charge flows through a resistor when there is a potential difference across it
items.misconception: Energy is transferred by heating when an object is at a high temperature
items.why: Students treat temperature as an absolute property of an object rather than something to compare with the surroundings. It is the difference that drives the transfer. Two objects at the same high temperature transfer no net energy to each other.
items.random_wrong: Gas flows out of a cylinder when the gas inside has a large volume

items.q: The weight of an object is directly proportional to its mass. What does this tell you?
items.correct: Doubling the mass doubles the weight in the same gravitational field
items.misconception: A graph of weight against mass is a straight line with a positive intercept
items.why: Students remember 'straight line' as the test for proportionality and drop the second half of the rule. A straight line with an intercept shows a constant rate of change, not proportionality. Doubling one quantity then does not double the other.
items.random_wrong: Weight and mass are the same quantity written in different units

items.q: A student loads a spring with increasing weights and finds that extension is directly proportional to force. Which statement about this model is correct?
items.correct: Doubling the force doubles the extension up to the limit of proportionality
items.misconception: Doubling the force doubles the extension for every force applied to the spring
items.why: Class experiments usually stay within the proportional region, so students never see the graph bend. Beyond the limit of proportionality the graph curves and equal increases in force give larger increases in extension. The proportional model has a stated range of validity.
items.random_wrong: Doubling the force doubles the extension only when the spring is unstretched

items.q: The specification says that physical laws and models are expressed in mathematical form. Which statement shows this key idea?
items.correct: weight = mass × gravitational field strength is a relationship
items.misconception: Rearranging an equation changes the physical law that it describes
items.why: Most classroom use of equations is substitution practice, so the relationship they express is easy to miss. Writing weight = mass × gravitational field strength states that weight is proportional to mass. The equation carries the physics; the arithmetic is a consequence of it.
items.random_wrong: An equation is only a shortcut for doing the arithmetic quickly

items.q: Does a useful model have to include every detail of the real thing?
items.correct: No. A model is deliberately simplified, and it is judged by how well it explains and predicts.
items.misconception: A model that leaves something out has been shown to be wrong and should be abandoned.
items.why: Students treat science as a collection of true statements, so any simplification looks like an error rather than a deliberate choice. Every model has limits. The particle model treats particles as tiny spheres with no internal structure; that simplification is what makes the model useful, and its limits show where a better model is needed.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do two magnets need a material between them in order to repel each other?
items.correct: No. A magnetic field acts through air and through a vacuum.
items.misconception: The air between the magnets is squashed and it is the air that pushes them apart.
items.why: Students look for a contact-force explanation, because every force they can feel directly involves touching something. Action at a distance is explained using the field. Each magnet sits in the field of the other, and the repulsion still happens with the air pumped away.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a magnet have a field when there is nothing nearby for it to attract?
items.correct: Yes. The field is a property of the magnet and is there whether or not a second object is present.
items.misconception: A field only appears at the moment a second object is brought close enough to feel a force.
items.why: Fields are invisible, so students accept them only when there is an observable force to point at. The field tells you the force a second object would feel if it were placed there. It exists in advance; the second object only reveals it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What drives charge to flow round a circuit?
items.correct: A potential difference across the component or the circuit.
items.misconception: Charge flows because a large amount of charge is stored in the cell, so the amount of charge is what matters.
items.why: The word charge appears in both ideas, and students picture a cell as a tank of charge that empties itself. The driver of change is the difference in potential, in the same way that a pressure difference drives gas flow and a temperature difference drives heating.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are weight and mass the same quantity?
items.correct: No. Weight is directly proportional to mass, with gravitational field strength as the constant of proportionality.
items.misconception: Weight and mass are two names for the same quantity, just written in different units.
items.why: In everyday speech people give weight in kilograms, and on one planet the two numbers really are in a fixed ratio. Weight is a force measured in newtons and mass is measured in kilograms. Proportionality links them; it does not make them identical, as a change of planet shows.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
